Let the Earth have radius \(1\), with coordinates
\[
(x,y,z)=(\cos\phi\cos\lambda,\cos\phi\sin\lambda,\sin\phi),
\]
where \(z\) points north.

The two points are at latitude \(30^\circ\), longitudes \(-45^\circ\) and \(45^\circ\):
\[
A=\left(\frac{\sqrt6}{4},-\frac{\sqrt6}{4},\frac12\right),
\qquad
B=\left(\frac{\sqrt6}{4},\frac{\sqrt6}{4},\frac12\right).
\]

The shortest path is the minor arc of the great circle through \(A\) and \(B\). By symmetry, its northernmost point is the midpoint of this minor arc, in the direction of \(A+B\):
\[
A+B=\left(\frac{\sqrt6}{2},0,1\right).
\]
Normalize this vector:
\[
\left|A+B\right|=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\right)^2+1^2}
=\sqrt{\frac64+1}
=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}.
\]
So the northernmost point has
\[
z=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}/2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{10}}=\sqrt{\frac25}.
\]
Since \(z=\sin\theta\), we get
\[
\sin\theta=\sqrt{\frac25}=\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}.
\]

The answer is \(\frac{\sqrt{10}}{5}\).
